explain.say: So: calm down, use I feel words, make a deal, do fun things together, and if it gets unsafe or unfair, ask a grown-up. Well done! Fun fact: in India, the festival Raksha Bandhan celebrates brothers and sisters.

faq.q: Why do siblings fight so much?
faq.a: Because they spend lots of time together and share rooms, toys and grown-ups' attention. Fighting is common, and learning to sort it out is a great life skill.
asks: Why do I fight with my brother so much?

faq.q: How can brothers and sisters make a deal?
faq.a: Sit down calmly, say what each of you needs, and agree a plan, like taking turns, set times, or rules for borrowing things.
asks: Tell me about the Make a deal

faq.q: What if my brother or sister hurts me?
faq.a: Move away and tell a parent, carer or another trusted adult straight away. Hurting is never okay, even between siblings.
asks: Tell me about the Ask a grown-up

faq.q: What if I feel my parents love my sibling more?
faq.a: That is a common feeling. Tell a parent how you feel; they can find special time just for you. Parents can love each child fully in different ways.
asks: Do my parents have a favourite?

faq.q: What if I am an only child?
faq.a: That is great too. Cousins, friends and neighbours can feel like siblings, and you can practise these skills with them.
asks: I do not have brothers or sisters

facts: During Raksha Bandhan, celebrated in India and Nepal, a sister ties a rakhi thread on her brother's wrist and he promises to protect her.
Research shows that siblings in childhood often spend more free time with each other than with their parents or friends.
